title: Encoding Categorical Features
html:
Most algorithms need numbers. The encoding must not invent an order that doesn't exist, must cope with categories never seen in training, and must not leak the target.

EncodingHowGood forWatch out
One-hotOne 0/1 column per categoryNominal features with few categories; linear modelsMany columns for high cardinality
OrdinalInteger code per category in a chosen orderTruly ordered categories (S < M < L); tree modelsImposes an order a linear model will take literally
Target (mean) encodingReplace each category by the (smoothed) target mean for itHigh-cardinality features (zip code, merchant)Leaks the target unless cross-fitted
Frequency / countReplace by how often the category occursHigh cardinality, tree modelsDifferent categories can collide on the same count
HashingHash category into a fixed number of columnsHuge or open-ended vocabularies, streamingCollisions; not reversible
EmbeddingsLearned dense vectorsVery high cardinality in neural netsNeeds a neural model (see Deep Learning)

One-hot and ordinal in scikit-learn

Watch out

Plain integer codes for a nominal feature (Delhi = 0, Mumbai = 1, Pune = 2) tell a linear model that Pune is “twice” Mumbai. Trees cope better with arbitrary codes, but one-hot or target encoding is usually safer. Never rely on alphabetical order for an ordinal feature — pass categories explicitly.

The dummy-variable trap

With an intercept, the full set of one-hot columns always sums to 1, so one column is a linear combination of the others (perfect multicollinearity). Unregularised linear regression then has no unique solution — use OneHotEncoder(drop="first"). With regularisation (Ridge, the default LogisticRegression) or tree models, keeping all columns is fine.

Many categories

target encoding(c) = (n_c · mean_c + m · global_mean) / (n_c + m) n_c = rows in category c, m = smoothing

Target encoding replaces each category by the mean target for that category, shrunk toward the global mean when the category is rare. Computed naively on the training rows it leaks each row's own label into its feature. scikit-learn's TargetEncoder avoids this with cross-fitting: fit_transform encodes each training row using statistics from the other folds, while transform on new data uses the full-training statistics.

How do you encode a feature with 10,000 categories?

Not with one-hot for a dense model. Options: target encoding with cross-fitting and smoothing, frequency encoding, hashing into a few thousand columns, grouping rare categories into “other”, or learned embeddings in a neural network. Tree libraries like LightGBM/CatBoost also handle categoricals natively.

How do you handle a category at prediction time that never appeared in training?

Decide up front: OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") encodes it as all zeros, infrequent-category grouping maps it to “other”, target encoders fall back to the global mean. Monitor how often unknown categories appear in production — a rising rate signals drift.
